tracks.legalName: Petition to Seal Records After Conviction (NRS 179.245)
tracks.publicName: Seal your Nevada conviction

controllingAuthority.summary: A person convicted in Nevada may petition the court in which they were convicted to seal all records relating to the conviction once the waiting period for the offence category has run. The periods are ten years for a category A felony, a crime of violence or residential burglary; five years for a category B, C or D felony; two years for a category E felony or a gross misdemeanour; seven years for non-felony Medicaid fraud, non-felony DUI or non-felony battery constituting domestic violence; two years for misdemeanour battery, harassment, stalking or a protective-order violation; and one year for any other misdemeanour. The trigger differs by paragraph: paragraphs (a) to (d) run from release from actual custody or discharge from parole or probation, whichever is later, while paragraphs (e) to (g) run from release from actual custody or from the end of a suspended sentence, whichever is later, and the eligibility engine must model both. NRS 179.2445 creates a rebuttable presumption that records should be sealed where the applicant satisfies all statutory requirements, except for a defendant dishonourably discharged from probation under NRS 176A.850, and if the prosecutor stipulates or fails to object within 30 days the court may seal without a hearing. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.

A violation of NRS 488.410 punishable as a felony under NRS 488.427, and violations of NRS 488.420 or 488.425.
Any case where the petitioner was charged with a pending offence, or convicted of any offence other than a minor moving or standing traffic violation, during the prescribed period. NRS 179.245(5).

destination.name: The district attorney's or city attorney's office first, then the clerk of the appropriate court
destination.detail: Nevada's workflow puts the prosecutor in the middle rather than at the end: the state's own instructions direct the petitioner to prepare the petition and order, submit them to the prosecuting agency with attachments, and file with the court clerk only after the prosecutor stipulates. Local practice is material. The Clark County District Attorney will not stipulate to petitions that include municipal court arrests or convictions, so a packet covering both must go to the appropriate city attorney and then to the district attorney, with a separate signature line for each prosecuting agency on the order. Only one petition, affidavit and order is required to seal all records within Clark County, and justice court petitions must be captioned to the specific township. Las Vegas Municipal Court requires its own Petition, Declaration and Verification, Order and Stipulation and denies typed signatures outright. Reno Municipal Court charges a filing fee, sets the petition for hearing at least 60 days after filing, and applies the sex trafficking fee exemption.

components.notes: Obtain a current verified criminal history from the Nevada Central Repository first. NRS 179.245(2)(a) and NRS 179.255(3)(a) make it a statutory attachment, so there is no packet without it. It requires fingerprints and carries a fee, which the NRS 179.245(9) sex trafficking waiver zeroes out where it applies.

Petition to seal records after conviction, generated to the county's template. The statutory content requirements at NRS 179.245(2) are the specification. Nevada has no statewide approved form: the Department of Public Safety publishes samples and every county district attorney, city attorney and municipal court runs its own packet, so the document is generated to a county-specific template. NRS 179.245(2) prescribes exactly what the petition must contain, which is what makes a generated pleading safe and auditable.

The proposed order, naming every agency to be served. In Clark County the order must carry a separate signature line for each prosecuting agency where the petition covers both municipal and justice or district court charges.

The affidavit or declaration and verification, required in every county reviewed. Las Vegas Municipal Court denies packets with typed rather than signed signatures immediately, so the signature block is left for the participant's hand.

components.conditionDescription: Where the county uses the stipulation route, which is the ordinary practice.
components.notes: The stipulation for the prosecutor's signature. This is the step that makes Nevada unusual: the state's own instructions direct the petitioner to submit the petition and order to the district attorney or city attorney first, and to file with the court clerk only after the prosecutor stipulates.

How to submit the packet to the correct prosecuting agency and what happens next. If the prosecutor stipulates, or fails to object within 30 days, the court may seal without a hearing. NRS 179.2445 creates a rebuttable presumption that records should be sealed where the applicant satisfies all statutory requirements, and NRS 179.245(4) requires the court to apply it both on a stipulation and at any contested hearing unless an objector rebuts it. The presumption does not apply to a defendant dishonourably discharged from probation under NRS 176A.850.

Filing with the clerk of the correct court, obtaining certified copies of the signed order, and serving every agency named in it. Under NRS 179.275 the order goes to the Central Repository and to the persons named, and the repository can take up to six months to complete its part, so the participant is told to expect that and to verify afterwards.

tracks.publicName: Seal a Nevada arrest that did not end in a conviction

controllingAuthority.summary: Where charges were dismissed the petition may be filed at any time after the dismissal; where prosecution was declined it may be filed at any time after the applicable statute of limitations has run, or any time eight years after the arrest, or pursuant to a stipulation between the parties; and where the person was acquitted it may be filed at any time after the acquittal. On an acquittal, and a finding that there is no evidence further action will be brought, the court shall order the records sealed, so relief is mandatory there; on a dismissal or declination it is discretionary but carries the NRS 179.2445 presumption. The NRS 179.245(6) conviction exclusions do not govern this track, so an arrest for an offence that could never be sealed as a conviction is still sealable where the case was dismissed or ended in acquittal. NRS 179.255(3)(b) adds an express requirement that the petition state the disposition of the proceedings. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.

controllingAuthority.summary: NRS 176.211 governs deferral of judgment and its own sealing. It has now been read in full and the mechanism is settled: sealing is automatic and court-ordered, and there is no participant filing. Under subsection 5, on completion of the terms and conditions and a finding by the court that they have been met, the court discharges the defendant and dismisses the proceedings. Under subsection 6, the court "shall order sealed all documents, papers and exhibits in the defendant's record, minute book entries and entries on dockets, and other documents relating to the case in the custody of such other agencies and officers as are named in the court's order", and "shall order those records sealed without a hearing unless the Division or the prosecutor petitions the court, for good cause shown, not to seal the records and requests a hearing thereon". Subsection 9(a) defines "court" for this section as a district court of the State of Nevada, so a justice court or municipal court matter is not on this route at all. The routing value of the node stands and is now supported rather than assumed: a participant will describe a deferred-judgment dismissal as an ordinary dismissal, and NRS 179.245 expressly excepts NRS 176.211 from the ordinary conviction petition, so sending them to a petition would be the wrong instrument for a remedy they are already entitled to receive without filing anything. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.

exclusions: NRS 176.211(7): the court may not order sealing under subsection 6 for a defendant who is charged with a violation of NRS 200.5099 (abuse, neglect, exploitation, isolation or abandonment of an older person or a vulnerable person) and who is discharged under the section. The deferral itself remains available; only the sealing is withheld.

Upstream, NRS 176.211(3)(b) bars deferral of judgment altogether for a defendant convicted of a violent or sexual offense as defined in NRS 202.876, a crime against a child as defined in NRS 179D.0357, a violation of NRS 200.508, or a violation of NRS 574.100 punishable under subsection 6 of that section. A person in any of those categories never reaches this route.
NRS 176.211(9)(a) confines the section to a district court of the State of Nevada. A deferral-like disposition in a justice court or a municipal court is not governed by this section.
Sealing under this section is not available where the deferral was terminated for violation of a term or condition and a judgment of conviction was entered under NRS 176.211(4).

tracks.legalName: Sealing After a Treatment-Program Discharge, Conditional Dismissal or Set-Aside (NRS 176A.245, 176A.265 and 176A.295)
tracks.publicName: Clearing a Nevada case after a court treatment programme, a conditional dismissal or a set-aside

controllingAuthority.summary: All three sections have now been read in full and they are structurally identical, differing only in the programme they attach to: NRS 176A.245 to the programme of treatment for alcohol or other substance use under NRS 176A.240, NRS 176A.265 to the programme for treatment of mental illness or intellectual disabilities under NRS 176A.260, and NRS 176A.295 to the programme for treatment of veterans and members of the military under NRS 176A.290. Each has two mechanisms, not one. Subsection 1 is automatic: after the defendant is discharged from probation or the case is dismissed under the corresponding programme section, the justice court, municipal court or district court, as applicable, "shall order sealed" the record if the defendant fulfilled the terms and conditions imposed by the court and the Division, and "shall order those records sealed without a hearing unless the Division petitions the court, for good cause shown, not to seal the records and requests a hearing thereon". Subsection 2 is not automatic: where the defendant was charged with a violation of NRS 200.485, NRS 484C.110 or NRS 484C.120 and the charges were conditionally dismissed or the judgment of conviction set aside, sealing follows only "not sooner than 7 years after" and "upon the filing of a petition by the defendant". So a participant filing does exist on this track, on a defined branch, with a defined waiting period. Subsection 3 of each section bars sealing where the defendant was charged with a violation of NRS 200.508 or NRS 200.5099. Subsection 4 requires the court to send a copy of the order to each agency or officer named in it, each of which must notify the court in writing of compliance. The grouping of the three sections into one track remains correct because the participant cannot be expected to know which programme section their case ran under, and the discharge-type screen remains load-bearing: NRS 179.2445(2) provides that the rebuttable presumption in favour of sealing does not apply to a defendant given a dishonorable discharge from probation under NRS 176A.850, which changes what that participant should expect on the ordinary conviction track. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.

exclusions: Subsection 3 of each of NRS 176A.245, 176A.265 and 176A.295: the court may not order sealing under the section where the defendant was charged with a violation of NRS 200.508 (abuse, neglect or endangerment of a child) or NRS 200.5099 (abuse, neglect, exploitation, isolation or abandonment of an older person or a vulnerable person), whether the defendant was discharged from probation, the case was dismissed, or the judgment of conviction was set aside.

The automatic sealing in subsection 1 does not reach a defendant who was charged with a violation of NRS 200.485 (battery constituting domestic violence), NRS 484C.110 or NRS 484C.120 and whose charges were conditionally dismissed or judgment of conviction set aside. Those matters are moved to the subsection 2 branch, which is not automatic and carries a seven-year wait.

The route depends on the case having run through the corresponding chapter 176A programme. A defendant who was never assigned to a programme under NRS 176A.240, NRS 176A.260 or NRS 176A.290 is not on this track.
Sealing under these sections is not available where the defendant failed the programme and was sentenced rather than discharged or dismissed.

destination.detail: On the subsection 1 branch the court acts on its own and the participant submits nothing. On the subsection 2 branch the participant files a petition in the court that handled the case — the sections name the justice court, municipal court or district court, as applicable, so venue follows the court of the underlying case rather than a single court level. Under subsection 4 the court sends a copy of any sealing order to each agency or officer named in it and each must notify the court in writing of compliance, and under NRS 179.275 a copy also goes to the Central Repository for Nevada Records of Criminal History.

components.notes: Detects which of the three chapter 176A programme sections applies — NRS 176A.245 for alcohol or other substance use treatment under NRS 176A.240, NRS 176A.265 for mental illness or intellectual disabilities under NRS 176A.260, NRS 176A.295 for veterans and members of the military under NRS 176A.290 — and then which branch applies within it. The section identity decides nothing about the mechanism, because all three are identical; the branch decides everything.

The single question that decides whether anything is generated at all: was the defendant charged with a violation of NRS 200.485, NRS 484C.110 or NRS 484C.120, and were the charges conditionally dismissed or the judgment of conviction set aside? If no, subsection 1 applies, sealing is automatic and nothing is filed. If yes, subsection 2 applies, sealing requires the defendant's petition and cannot be sought sooner than seven years after.

Whether the discharge from probation was honourable or dishonourable. NRS 179.2445(2) provides that the rebuttable presumption in favour of sealing does not apply to a defendant given a dishonorable discharge under NRS 176A.850 who applies for sealing of records relating to the conviction, which changes what the participant should expect on the ordinary conviction track. It does not change the mechanism on this track, where subsections 1 and 2 turn on fulfilment of the terms and conditions rather than on the presumption.

components.conditionDescription: Generated only on the subsection 2 branch: a violation of NRS 200.485, NRS 484C.110 or NRS 484C.120, conditionally dismissed or the judgment of conviction set aside, and not sooner than seven years after.
components.notes: The petition by the defendant that subsection 2 of NRS 176A.245, NRS 176A.265 or NRS 176A.295 requires. There is no official statewide form: the Nevada State Police Records, Communications and Compliance Division publishes only a General Information document and two sample petitions for the ordinary chapter 179 sealing petition, and records that procedures vary from county to county. The petition pleads the programme section the case ran under, the conditional dismissal or set-aside and its date, that seven years have elapsed, that the defendant fulfilled the terms and conditions imposed by the court and the Division, and that no subsection 3 exclusion applies, and asks the court to order the records sealed under the applicable subsection 2.

An order sealing all documents, papers and exhibits in the defendant's record, minute book entries and entries on dockets, and other documents relating to the case in the custody of the agencies and officers named in it. The order must name those custodians, because subsection 1 and subsection 2 both reach only records "in the custody of such other agencies and officers as are named in the court's order", and because subsection 4 makes each named agency report its compliance to the court.

The participant's own statement of the facts the petition asserts: the programme, the disposition and its date, the seven-year computation, and fulfilment of the terms and conditions. The sections prescribe no verification; this is the ordinary support for facts not appearing of record.

Where to file — the justice court, municipal court or district court that handled the case — and what to expect: the court shall order the records sealed without a hearing unless the Division petitions for good cause not to seal and requests one. The sections prescribe no service and name no fee; the instructions must say that rather than invent either.
Where to go on the automatic branch, where nothing is filed: the court that supervised the programme, which holds the sealing order and is the only body that can act, and Nevada Legal Services.

On the subsection 2 branch the defendant files a petition in the court that handled the case, and not sooner than seven years after the conditional dismissal or the setting aside of the judgment.
rules.fees: None is prescribed. Neither NRS 176A.245, NRS 176A.265 nor NRS 176A.295 imposes, authorises or mentions a fee, on either branch. Whether a particular clerk charges a filing fee for the subsection 2 petition is not established by the sections and is recorded as an open question rather than asserted either way. The NRS 179.245(9) sex-trafficking fee waiver is confined by its own words to a petition for sealing under NRS 179.245 and does not by its terms reach these sections.
rules.feeWaiver: None prescribed by these sections. NRS 179.245(9) waives fees related to a petition for sealing under NRS 179.245 where the petitioner was being sex trafficked when the crime was committed; its text is confined to that section and it is not authority for a waiver here.
rules.notice: No notice duty falls on the participant on either branch. Under subsection 4 the court sends a copy of any sealing order to each agency or officer named in it and each must notify the court in writing of compliance, and under NRS 179.275 a copy also goes to the Central Repository and each named custodian.
rules.service: The sections prescribe none. On the subsection 1 branch there is nothing to serve. On the subsection 2 branch the sections require only "the filing of a petition by the defendant" and name no person to be served; the Division is the body given the right to object, and whether the petition must be served on it or on the prosecutor is not established by the text and is recorded as an open question.
rules.participantSignature: On the subsection 2 branch the petitioner signs the petition and the declaration personally. On the subsection 1 branch nothing is generated for the participant to sign.
rules.notarization: None required. The sections prescribe no verification or notarization.

The Division of Parole and Probation petitions the court, for good cause shown, not to seal and requests a hearing. That is a contested proceeding.
Whether the defendant fulfilled the terms and conditions imposed by the court and the Division is disputed or unclear on the record; that is the condition on which both branches turn.
The programme was not completed and the defendant was sentenced rather than discharged or the case dismissed.

The seven-year period under subsection 2 has not elapsed, or its start date is uncertain because the record does not show clearly whether the disposition was a conditional dismissal, a set-aside or an ordinary dismissal.
Any dishonourable discharge, which under NRS 179.2445(2) removes the presumption on any later petition under NRS 179.245.

Any offence-category question. Nevada eligibility turns on category A through E felony, gross misdemeanour or misdemeanour and on whether the offence is a crime of violence, which is a legal classification driving a one-year versus ten-year answer on the ordinary tracks.
Any pending charge, and any conviction during the clean period other than a minor moving or standing traffic violation.
Records in more than one county, or in both municipal and justice or district court, where practice differs by court and prosecuting agency.
Federal, tribal, military and out-of-state records.

tracks.legalName: Removal of a Record from the Central Repository After a Favourable Disposition (NRS 179A.160)
tracks.publicName: Getting a Nevada arrest off the state repository after a favourable outcome

controllingAuthority.summary: NRS 179A.160 has now been read in full and it is not a route on which nothing is filed. Subsection 1 provides that where a person has been arrested or issued a citation, or has been the subject of a warrant for alleged criminal conduct, and is acquitted or the disposition of the charge is favourable to the person, then "at any time after the charge is dismissed, acquittal is entered or disposition of the charge in favor of the person is final, the person who is the subject of a record of criminal history relating to the arrest, citation or warrant may apply in writing to the Central Repository and the agency which maintains the record to have it removed from the files which are available and generally searched for the purpose of responding to inquiries concerning the criminal history of a person." Subsection 2 makes removal mandatory — "The Central Repository and the agency shall remove the record unless" one of five stated conditions applies. So the participant makes a written application, to two recipients, with no waiting period and no hearing, and the agencies must act unless an exclusion bites. It remains a repository remedy rather than a court sealing order, so it sits alongside the NRS 179.255 petition rather than replacing it, and subsection 3 preserves a court's separate authority to order deletion or modification of a record. Nevada calls it record sealing and never expungement: the Department of Public Safety states directly that sealing is not expungement because it does not authorise destruction of the records, and NRS 179A.160 likewise removes a record from the files that are available and generally searched rather than destroying it. Under NRS 179.285 the proceedings are deemed never to have occurred and civil rights are restored, but NRS 179.295 allows sealed records to be reopened and NRS 179.301 allows certain persons and agencies to inspect them. A Nevada order does not bind out-of-state or federal agencies and does not reach records they hold. Sealing does not restore firearm rights; only a pardon that does not restrict the right to bear arms does.

exclusions: NRS 179A.160(2)(a): the person is a fugitive.
NRS 179A.160(2)(b): the case is under active prosecution according to a current certificate of a prosecuting attorney.

NRS 179A.160(2)(c): the disposition of the case was a deferred prosecution, plea bargain or other similar disposition. This is the exclusion that most often defeats the route in practice and it is why a participant whose case was resolved by a deferral of judgment belongs on the NRS 176.211 track and not here.
NRS 179A.160(2)(d): the person has a prior conviction for a felony or gross misdemeanour in any jurisdiction in the United States — not merely in Nevada.
NRS 179A.160(2)(e): the person has been arrested for or charged with another crime, other than a minor traffic violation, since the arrest, citation or warrant which the person seeks to have removed.

waitingPeriods.condition: None. NRS 179A.160(1) permits the application "at any time after the charge is dismissed, acquittal is entered or disposition of the charge in favor of the person is final". The only temporal condition is that the favourable disposition be final.
waitingPeriods.duration: none

geography.venue: Not a filing route. The court or agency that handled the matter holds the record.

destination.name: The Central Repository for Nevada Records of Criminal History, and the agency which maintains the record
destination.detail: NRS 179A.160(1) directs the application to two recipients and not one: the Central Repository for Nevada Records of Criminal History, administered by the Nevada State Police Records, Communications and Compliance Division at 333 West Nye Lane, Suite 100, Carson City, Nevada 89706, and the agency which maintains the record, ordinarily the arresting agency. The application is made in writing by the person who is the subject of the record. It is not a court filing, no order issues on it, and it does not reach the court's own record, which is why the parallel screen for the court sealing petition matters.

components.notes: The written application under NRS 179A.160(1). No official form exists: the Nevada State Police Records, Communications and Compliance Division publishes only a General Information document, a statutory information page and two sample petitions for the ordinary chapter 179 court sealing petition, none of which addresses this section, and the section itself prescribes no form. The application identifies the applicant and any former names, identifies the arrest, citation or warrant by agency, date and case or event number, states the favourable disposition and the date it became final, asks that the record be removed from the files which are available and generally searched for the purpose of responding to criminal history inquiries, and addresses each of the five subsection 2 conditions so the agency can act on the face of the application.

The same written application, addressed to the agency which maintains the record. Subsection 1 requires the application to go to the Central Repository and the agency, and subsection 2 puts the removal duty on both. A single copy sent to the Repository alone leaves the arresting agency's own record untouched, which is exactly the failure this node exists to prevent.

What the repository remedy is and how it differs from a court sealing order: it addresses the state's own criminal history record and the record-holding agency's, not the court's, and it removes the record from the files that are available and generally searched rather than destroying it. Subsection 3 preserves the court's separate authority, so the two remedies coexist.

The parallel screen under the non-conviction sealing track, which is a court petition the participant can pursue. This is the point of the node in the other direction: repository removal alone leaves the court record. The Records, Communications and Compliance Division's own General Information document, rev. 8/2025, records that the sealing process can take up to 6 months to complete once the final seal order is received, so a participant who obtains a court order should not expect the repository to reflect it at once.

Screens each of the five NRS 179A.160(2) conditions before anything is generated. Two of them are easy for a participant to get wrong: a deferred prosecution, plea bargain or other similar disposition defeats the route even though the participant will describe the outcome as favourable, and a prior felony or gross misdemeanour conviction anywhere in the United States defeats it even though the participant may be thinking only of Nevada.
How to approach the Records, Communications and Compliance Division and the record-holding agency, and where to get help, including Nevada Legal Services.

That section directs the distribution of a sealing order to the Central Repository and to each named custodian and says nothing about timing. The six-month figure comes from the Records, Communications and Compliance Division's own General Information document, rev. 8/2025, which states that the process can take up to 6 months to complete once the final seal order is received; the Division's web page currently gives 2 to 4 months for the same process. _sealingMechanismCorrection.feeWaiverScopeCorrection: The track previously recorded that any repository fee is waived for a victim of sex trafficking or involuntary servitude under NRS 179.245(9). Read in full, subsection 9 waives fees "related to a petition for the sealing of records pursuant to this section", which is NRS 179.245 and not this one. The waiver is real and is preserved on the tracks it governs; it is not authority for a waiver here, and in any event NRS 179A.160 prescribes no fee. Nevada holds no 2026 session. The text read on 2026-08-08 is therefore the whole of the current law, with no session gap of the kind that has to be closed separately in annual-session states.
_sealingMechanismCorrection.boundary: Boundary of this correction: it establishes the governing mechanism, the automatic-versus-participant-filed question, the vehicle, the destination, the exclusions, the waiting periods, the notice, the service, the fee, the hearing, the prosecutor role, the proposed-order role, the output strategy and the packet-capability classification for this track from the operative statutory text. It enables nothing: the track remains runtime disabled and not packet ready, no packet is implemented, no renderer is written, no official form is created or acquired, no source is materialized and no shared registry or composed approval is touched. The six completed Nevada custom-pleading tracks and their implemented module are untouched and value-identical.
openQuestionsCreatedByThisCorrection: What makes a disposition "favorable to the person" for the purposes of NRS 179A.160(1). The section does not define it and the five subsection 2 exclusions define the negative rather than the positive. Recorded as a self-help stop: it changes who is eligible, not what is generated.

legalDesignDecision.rationale: The review's decision was "Process guidance only", recorded without the section's text, and reading the section shows the classification cannot stand. NRS 179A.160(1) gives the participant an express written application, to two named recipients, available at any time after a favourable disposition becomes final; subsection 2 makes removal mandatory unless one of five stated conditions applies. That is a participant filing whose content the statute prescribes, and there is no official form for it, so the correct output strategy is custom_pleading. The guidance rationales no_participant_filing_exists and another_entity_decides are removed: the first is contradicted by the section, and the second would classify every application to any agency as guidance, which is precisely the reasoning the correction assignment forbids. What the node already had right is kept and strengthened. The parallel screen remains the most valuable thing on the track, because repository removal alone leaves the court record and a court order alone does not reach the repository at once, and the five statutory exclusions — particularly the deferred-prosecution and plea-bargain exclusion, and the prior-conviction exclusion that reaches the whole United States — are now screened before anything is generated instead of being left to a warning.
